rules.sentence: Ulnar neuropathy at the wrist and hand may manifest as purely sensory, purely motor, or mixed deficits.
Type I lesions occur just proximal to or within the Guyon canal, affecting both deep and superficial branches, producing mixed motor and sensory deficits with weakness of all ulnar hand muscles.
Type II lesions involve the deep branch exclusively, causing a pure motor deficit with a variable pattern of weakness depending on the compression site.
Type III lesions are limited to the superficial branch, resulting in purely sensory deficits of the palmar aspect of the medial one-half of the fourth digit and the fifth digit.
Diagnosis of ulnar neuropathy traditionally depends on clinical history, physical examination, and electrodiagnostic studies.

Combined use of electromyography and nerve conduction studies improves diagnostic accuracy by localizing sites of pathological compression, allowing relatively early identification in patients with symptoms indicative of ulnar nerve lesions.

A recent meta-analysis demonstrated that in healthy participants, the ulnar nerve cross-sectional area at various locations around the elbow rarely exceeds 10 mm, providing a potential cutoff for diagnosing ulnar nerve entrapment in this region.[27]
